1.title: Training and Fine-Tuning Foundation Models
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: Training and Fine-Tuning Foundation Models. This module covers task statement three point three. You will learn how foundation models are trained, the main ways to adapt a pre-trained model, and how to prepare the data. The exam gives you the data you have, or the goal you want, and asks you to name the method or the preparation step.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. Describe the key elements of training a foundation model: pre-training, fine-tuning, continued pre-training and distillation. Define the methods for fine-tuning: instruction tuning, domain adaptation and transfer learning. And describe how to prepare data: curation, governance, size, labeling, representativeness, and R L H F.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedar and Salt Considers Training
1.text: At Cedar and Salt Travel, prompts and R A G help, but the team wants the model to write in the company's own style. They hold thousands of labeled review summaries and many internal manuals. Chat is costly on a large model, and some of the data holds guest details. Your job is to choose the method and prepare the data the right way.

1.title: Training a Foundation Model: The Key Elements
1.text: Start with pre-training. A model learns from a broad body of unlabeled data, using self-supervised learning, which creates labels from the input itself. Building one from scratch can cost millions of dollars, so most teams start from a pre-trained model. Adaptation then makes it fit your needs: fine-tuning, continued pre-training and distillation. Common training settings are epochs, the passes through the data, the learning rate, which sets how fast the weights change, and the batch size. In Amazon Bedrock, training is billed on tokens processed times epochs, plus storage. Exam tip: pre-training learns general language from unlabeled data, and adaptation makes it fit.

1.title: The Ways to Adapt a Pre-Trained Model
1.text: The picture shows one pre-trained model with four paths. Fine-tuning uses labeled prompt and response pairs, for a specific task. Continued pre-training uses unlabeled text from your domain. Distillation lets a smaller student learn from a larger teacher. And R L H F uses human rankings to steer the model toward preferred answers. Fine-tuning and continued pre-training change the model's weights. Exam tip: the type of data decides the method. Is it labeled, unlabeled, teacher output or human ranking?

1.title: Fine-Tuning and Instruction Tuning
1.text: Fine-tuning trains a pre-trained model further, to improve performance on specific tasks. Instruction tuning is a kind of fine-tuning that uses labeled examples, formatted as prompt and response pairs, phrased as instructions. It changes the model's weights. Use it when prompt engineering is not enough, for business-specific needs, domain jargon and better task results. Models such as Flan T five are tuned this way, and they do better at zero-shot tasks; they can be tuned further. Fine-tuning needs labeled data. Exam tip: labeled prompt and response pairs for one task means fine-tuning, or instruction tuning.

1.title: Domain Adaptation and Continued Pre-Training
1.text: Domain adaptation adapts a pre-trained model to domain-specific language, such as industry jargon and technical terms. It uses plain, unlabeled text from the domain, such as reports and manuals. Continued pre-training in Amazon Bedrock also uses unlabeled data, to make a model more domain-specific. Both modify the weights, and neither needs labels. As of five November twenty twenty-six, the Amazon Bedrock customization page lists supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement fine-tuning and distillation, so check which methods your model supports. Exam tip: unlabeled domain text to learn vocabulary means domain adaptation, or continued pre-training.

1.title: Transfer Learning and Distillation
1.text: Transfer learning means a model pre-trained on one task is fine-tuned for a new, related task. It is faster, and needs less data and compute. Distillation is different: a larger teacher model passes knowledge to a smaller, faster student, giving you a cheaper, quicker model for your use case. In Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation, the teacher responses come from your prompts or from invocation logs, and they fine-tune the student. Teacher calls can add on-demand charges, and only you can access the distilled model. Exam tip: reuse a pre-trained model for a new task is transfer learning; smaller and cheaper is distillation.

1.title: Preparing Data to Fine-Tune
1.text: Now data preparation, with five concerns. Data curation: select relevant, accurate examples, and remove errors and duplicates. Governance: confirm you may use the data, protect personal information, and control access. Size: enough examples for the task; the limits vary by model, and you should hold out a validation set. Labeling: pair each prompt with a correct, consistent response. And representativeness: cover the real mix of tasks, languages and users, to avoid bias. Exam tip: quality, governance and coverage beat raw volume.

1.title: Fine-Tuning Data in Practice
1.text: What does the data look like in practice? Amazon Bedrock takes training data as J S O N Lines files, with one record per line. A training dataset is required, and a validation dataset is optional for many models. Text tasks use a prompt field and a completion field, while chat models use system, user and assistant messages. Store the files in Amazon S three, and plan size at about six characters per token. Your inputs and customizations stay private to your A W S account, and are not shared with model providers. Exam tip: fine-tuning data is labeled, in prompt and completion form, and kept private.

1.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)
1.text: R L H F, reinforcement learning from human feedback, uses human feedback to align a model with human preferences. It has four steps. One: collect data, where people write prompts and good responses. Two: fine-tune a pre-trained model on those pairs. Three: build a reward model, where people rank several responses and the rankings train the reward model. Four: optimize, so the model uses the reward model to favor higher-rated answers. It helps with qualities that are hard to measure, such as helpful, harmless and friendly. Exam tip: humans rank answers to train a reward model means R L H F.

1.title: Which Method for Which Data?
1.text: Which method fits which data? Labeled prompt and response pairs for one task: fine-tuning, or instruction tuning. Unlabeled text from your domain: domain adaptation or continued pre-training. A large teacher model and a need for a cheaper one: distillation. Human rankings of answers: R L H F. A pre-trained model and a new, related task: transfer learning. And vast unlabeled data with large budgets: pre-training. Exam tip: look at the data first, then name the method.

1.title: What the Exam Asks: Training and Fine-Tuning
1.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. Which element: pre-training, fine-tuning, continued pre-training or distillation. Which method: instruction tuning, domain adaptation or transfer learning. Which data: labeled for fine-tuning, and unlabeled for continued pre-training. Which preparation step: curation, governance, size, labeling or representativeness. And which technique uses people: R L H F. Exam tip: name the data first, then the method.

1.title: Design Check: Cedar and Salt's Training Plan
1.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and name the answer. Thousands of labeled review summaries: fine-tuning, or instruction tuning. Many internal manuals with no labels: domain adaptation or continued pre-training. Chat costs too much on a large model: distillation to a smaller student. Replies must feel friendly, as rated by staff: R L H F. Training data holds guest names and emails: governance, so remove or protect the personal data. And examples only in English while guests are global: representativeness, so add other languages. Pause the video if you want more time.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. The training elements are pre-training, fine-tuning, continued pre-training and distillation. The methods are instruction tuning, domain adaptation and transfer learning. The data decides: labeled for fine-tuning, unlabeled for domain adaptation, and human rankings for R L H F. Preparation covers curation, governance, size, labeling and representativeness. And in Amazon Bedrock, your data stays private to your account.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Which description fits the pre-training of a foundation model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: training on a broad body of unlabeled data for general ability. Pre-training uses generalized, unlabeled data and self-supervised learning. The other options describe fine-tuning, distillation and R L H F.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Cedar and Salt holds two thousand labeled examples of ideal review summaries. Which approach best improves the model on this one task? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: fine-tuning with labeled prompt and response pairs. Fine-tuning, or instruction tuning, improves performance on a specific task. Distillation shrinks a model, continued pre-training uses unlabeled text, and pre-training from scratch is the most costly.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Select two. Which two are considerations when preparing data to fine-tune a foundation model? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Data should be curated, governed, labeled and representative of real use. Volume without quality does not help, fine-tuning uses labeled data, and unchecked copying risks errors, bias and rights problems.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Cedar and Salt wants a smaller, cheaper model to match the quality of a large model on its chat prompts. Which technique fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: model distillation, with a large teacher and a small student. Distillation transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller, faster, more cost-efficient one. The other options do not produce a smaller model.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. In R L H F, what do human evaluators do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: they rank responses, so a reward model learns preferences. The rankings train the reward model, which the language model then uses to favor higher-rated answers.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A company wants a model to learn its industry jargon from a large collection of unlabeled manuals. Which method fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: domain adaptation or continued pre-training on the text. These use unlabeled domain text to teach vocabulary and context. Instruction tuning needs labeled pairs, distillation needs a teacher, and R L H F needs human rankings.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: B. Question two: C. Question three: A and C. Question four: A. Question five: D. Question six: B. That completes Module nine. Next, Module ten looks at how to evaluate foundation model performance, with metrics and benchmarks.
